content: The Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act (SARA) was signed into law by President Ronald Reagan on October 17, 1986. This act amended the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (CERCLA), commonly referred to as Superfund. A separate law, the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act of 1986 (EPCRA), was included as Title III of SARA. The primary purpose of EPCRA is to promote and support emergency planning at state and local levels while providing the public and local governments with information about potential chemical hazards in their communities. EPCRA Reporting Requirements EPCRA does not restrict the storage, use, release, disposal, or transfer of chemicals at a facility. Instead, it mandates that facilities document, notify, and report specific information. Each section of the law imposes different requirements, deadlines, and applies to distinct groups of chemicals. Emergency Planning (Sections 301-303) These sections ensure that state and local communities are prepared to respond to potential chemical accidents. Each state is required to establish a State Emergency Response Commission (SERC), which designates local emergency planning districts. For each district, the SERC appoints and oversees a Local Emergency Planning Committee (LEPC). The LEPC is responsible for developing an emergency response plan for its district and reviewing it annually. The LEPC must include representatives from public and private organizations, as well as a representative from every facility subject to EPCRA emergency planning requirements. The emergency response plan developed by the LEPC must: Identify affected facilities and transportation routes. Describe emergency notification and response procedures. Designate community and facility emergency coordinators. Outline methods to determine the occurrence and extent of a chemical release. Identify available response equipment and personnel. Include evacuation plans. Describe training and practice programs and schedules. Contain methods and schedules for exercising the plan. Facilities subject to EPCRA emergency planning requirements are determined based on the presence of extremely hazardous substances (EHS) listed by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Each EHS has a threshold planning quantity (TPQ), expressed in pounds. If a facility has an amount of an EHS equal to or exceeding its TPQ, it must notify the SERC and LEPC and appoint an emergency response coordinator to collaborate with the LEPC on the local emergency plan. Emergency Release Notification (Section 304) Facilities may be subject to these reporting requirements even if they are not covered by Sections 301-303. This section applies to any facility that stores, produces, or uses a hazardous chemical (defined as a chemical posing a physical or health hazard) and releases a reportable quantity (RQ) of a substance listed in either of the following EPA-published tables: List of extremely hazardous substances. List of CERCLA hazardous substances. The RQ, expressed in pounds, determines whether a release must be reported. If the amount of a chemical released into the environment exceeds the RQ, the facility must immediately report the release to the appropriate LEPC and SERC and provide a written follow-up as soon as possible. Exceptions include releases that result in exposure solely within the facility boundary or federally permitted releases. Continuous pesticide and radionuclide releases meeting specific conditions are also exempt. Community Right-to-Know Reporting Requirements (Sections 311-312) These requirements aim to increase community awareness of chemical hazards and facilitate emergency planning. They apply to any facility required by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) to prepare or maintain a Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) for a hazardous chemical or that has on-site, for any one day in a calendar year, an amount of a hazardous chemical equal to or greater than: 10,000 pounds for hazardous chemicals. The lesser of 500 pounds or the TPQ for extremely hazardous substances. Facilities subject to these requirements must submit information to the SERC, LEPC, and local fire department under two categories: MSDS reporting and inventory reporting. MSDS Reporting: Facilities must provide: Initially, a copy of the MSDS for each chemical exceeding the threshold or a list of such chemicals grouped into categories. Within three months of any change, an MSDS or list for additional chemicals meeting the reporting criteria. Inventory Reporting: Facilities must provide information on the amounts, locations, and storage conditions of hazardous chemicals and mixtures containing hazardous chemicals. The inventory report has two forms: Tier One Form: Contains aggregate information for applicable hazard categories and must be submitted annually by March 1st. Tier Two Form: Provides more detailed information, including the specific names of each chemical, and is submitted upon request by authorized agencies or annually in place of the Tier One Form. Toxic Chemical Release Inventory Reporting (Section 313) This section supports research and the development of regulations, guidelines, and standards. The EPA is required to establish the Toxics Release Inventory (TRI), which tracks routine toxic chemical emissions from certain facilities. The original TRI data requirements, specified in SARA Title III, were expanded by the Pollution Prevention Act of 1990 to include information on source reduction, recycling, and treatment. Facilities must submit a Toxic Chemical Release Inventory Form (Form R) to the EPA and designated state officials annually by July 1st if they: Have 10 or more full-time employees. Operate in a specified Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) Code. Manufacture, process, or otherwise use listed toxic chemicals in quantities exceeding specific thresholds (e.g., 25,000 pounds per year for manufacturing or processing, or 10,000 pounds per year for other uses). In December 2006, the EPA finalized a new TRI rule expanding eligibility for the use of the Form A Certification Statement as an alternative to the more detailed Form R. The list of toxic chemicals subject to reporting under this section is routinely updated. Federal Agency Responsibilities Under EPCRA Since April 30, 1993, the United States Air Force has voluntarily complied with Sections 303 and 304 of EPCRA, despite federal facilities initially being exempt from its requirements. However, on August 3, 1993, President Clinton signed Executive Order 12856, mandating federal agencies, including the Department of Defense, to fully comply with all provisions of EPCRA and the Pollution Prevention Act, except for the reporting requirements under Section 313. Unlike non-federal facilities, federal agencies must comply with Section 313 provisions regardless of the SIC code applicable to their facilities.
